cells.tense: You are standing where the care is already doing its work, and it shows in what grows.
cells.ask: Leave one thing you are holding well alone for a day — no adjusting, no checking — and see whether it holds without your hand on it.
cells.core:
You're tending something and it's growing. Not because you're pushing it — because you've stopped. Holding on and holding space are different, and right now you're doing the second one. Whatever is in your care gets room to move, and then it moves. That's how you know it's working.

Part of what makes it work is that you spend your attention where it lands and leave the rest be. People around you settle. They bring things to you without bracing first. The care isn't costing you more than it should, and you're still in the room rather than emptied by it. What you know to attend to and what you actually attend to have lined up, at least here.

None of that stays true on its own. It holds because you keep letting things finish without you standing over them.
cells.sheetLine: The care is working because you let things finish without you.

cells.tense: You are already bracing for a version of this that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're managing right now and leave it unattended for a day, then notice what it did on its own.
cells.core:
The care has turned into management. You're watching for the next thing to go wrong, the next gap to close. It feels like love from the inside. From the outside it looks like a hand that won't let go. You know what needs tending. That's not the problem. The problem is that everything gets tended before it asks.

You take the shape of what someone might need before they've said a word, and you're already carrying it. But the thing in front of you doesn't need tomorrow's hands. It needs to be left alone long enough to show you what it does by itself. It might stand. It might not. Either is information you can't get while you're holding it up. The managing is costing you the very thing it was for.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding things that haven't asked to be held.

cells.tense: You were standing at a door some time back, and part of you is still there.
cells.ask: Give fifteen unhurried minutes to one small thing that catches your attention — no plan, no outcome. Repeat once this week.
cells.core:
Something stopped growing, and the care stopped landing anywhere it could take root. Calling that independence is fair enough. But knowing what to attend to is still yours — it just isn't running right now. Something catches your eye, and you look away, and that's the whole exchange.

More effort pushed into the quiet place won't help. One thing allowed to pull might. Not because it's owed. Because something is worth turning toward, and the turning itself does the work. Attention given to something small starts the current again. The rest tends to follow.

Pick the thing that keeps catching your eye even after you've looked away, and give it the minutes you'd otherwise spend managing nothing.
cells.sheetLine: Stop pushing the care. Let one thing pull instead.

cells.tense: You are carrying a role that nobody handed you, and you are already inside it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you do for someone and say out loud that you picked it — or don't pick it this once, and let it stay undone.
cells.core:
People come to you as someone who holds things. You didn't sign up for that, but you're doing it, and somewhere along the way the doing became the shape rather than something you laid down at night. You know what needs your attention. That part isn't in question. What's in question is whether you've noticed you're the one deciding.

The care is doing real work on the people around you. What's gone quiet is the part where it gets said out loud that you chose it. You don't have to stop being the one people lean on — but you could start being the one who knows they're leaning. That's not a small shift. It's the difference between being used up and being spent on purpose.

One act named as yours starts it. The rest can stay exactly where it is for now.
cells.sheetLine: You didn't choose the role. You can choose what stays in it.

attempts.check: The record supports care-as-capacity in a Wisdom seat, but not the claim that the person actually feels depleted or has been cast as a caretaker by others — that is the record's label, not a fact about them. A reader could reasonably say 'nobody made me the caretaker; I chose this,' and the cell must let them say it and still walk away with something to use. The ask survives being wrong — it is one small act, not a verdict on their history. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line that tells them what they feel, so those are gone.
